results.content: 4. Modeling County-Level Rare Disease Preva ... # Journal of Data Science. Modeling County-Level Rare Disease Prevalence Using Bayesian Hierarchical Sampling Weighted Zero-Inflated Regression✩. ✩ The findings and conclusions in this report are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Estimates of county-level disease prevalence have a variety of applications. Such estimation is often done via model-based small-area estimation using survey data. However, for conditions with low prevalence (i.e., rare diseases or newly diagnosed diseases), counties with a high fraction of zero counts in surveys are common. Using single-year survey data, we proposed a Bayesian weighted Binomial Zero-inflated (BBZ) model to estimate county-level rare diseases prevalence. The BBZ model accounts for excess zero counts, the sampling weights and uses a power prior. The problem of rarity: estimation of prevalence in rare disease. A comparison of model-based methods for small area estimation.

results.title: The Analytic Network Process (ANP) Method: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Advantages, and Limitations
results.content: # The Analytic Network Process (ANP) Method: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Advantages, and Limitations. In today's increasingly complex decision-making environments, organizations, governments, and industries must evaluate multiple criteria simultaneously to arrive at optimal solutions. As a result, advanced multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methodologies have gained widespread prominence. Among them, the Analytic Network Process (ANP) has emerged as a powerful tool, offering a structured yet flexible approach for evaluating complex decision problems. By the end of this review, readers will have a robust understanding of how ANP facilitates well-informed, data-driven decisions across diverse industries. ANP is a generalized form of AHP that incorporates interdependencies among decision elements. * Non-linearity: Unlike AHP, ANP accommodates loops, cycles, and complex relationships within decision problems. * Pairwise comparisons are conducted between: Criteria affecting the decision Interdependent elements within clusters Alternatives in relation to each criterion. * The super-matrix represents all relationships within the decision network. Given its ability to handle complex decision-making scenarios, ANP has been widely adopted in numerous fields. * Product design optimization: ANP is used to evaluate design criteria such as cost, performance, and sustainability. * Disaster risk management: ANP evaluates potential mitigation strategies for earthquakes, floods, and other disasters. While ANP is a powerful decision-making tool, it is not without challenges. * Captures complex relationships: Unlike AHP, ANP accounts for dependencies between decision criteria. * Hybrid models: Combining ANP with other decision-making methods such as TOPSIS, DEMATEL, and Fuzzy Logic to enhance accuracy. * Real-time decision support systems: Developing software solutions that integrate ANP for instant analysis in dynamic decision environments. * Big Data integration: Incorporating ANP into large-scale data analytics for improved decision-making in business intelligence. Conclusion: Why ANP is a Game-Changer in Decision-Making. The Analytic Network Process (ANP) represents a significant advancement in decision-making methodologies by addressing the limitations of hierarchical models like AHP. From engineering and healthcare to finance and sustainability, ANP has proven its effectiveness in tackling multi-dimensional decision challenges. As decision-making becomes more complex, incorporating ANP into AI-driven models, hybrid methodologies, and real-time analytics will unlock even greater potential. Researchers and practitioners alike should continue exploring its capabilities to make better, data-driven, and informed decisions in the years ahead.
